crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Rolling Forecasts
children.blurb: A rolling forecast is a planning process that continuously updates projections for a fixed future period, such as twelve or eighteen months, rather than stopping at the fiscal year end.

children.name: External Signals in Revenue Models
children.blurb: External signals in revenue models are data points from outside the company that affect future revenue, including competitor disclosures, merger and acquisition filings, regulatory changes, litigation activity, and market instruments tied to AI.

children.name: Variance Analysis and Explanation
children.blurb: Variance analysis and explanation covers the comparison of planned or forecast figures against actual results, and the work of identifying why differences occurred.

children.name: Capital Spending Decisions
children.blurb: Capital spending decisions in AI accounting cover how an organization plans, approves, and monitors long-term investments in AI-related assets, including compute hardware, data infrastructure, software licenses, and the staff or services needed to operate them.

children.name: Zero-Based Budgeting
children.blurb: Zero-based budgeting is a planning method where every expense must be justified for each new period, starting from a zero base rather than the previous budget.

sections.body: Forecasting and planning is the part of accounting where a company tries to predict revenue, costs, and cash needs before they happen. Artificial intelligence is now doing real work in this area, not just theoretical modeling. Rolling forecasts are updated automatically as new transactions arrive, so the forecast always reflects the latest month or week instead of a fixed annual budget. Revenue models pull in external signals such as foot traffic, shipping volumes, or commodity prices and use them to adjust predictions. Variance analysis tools compare what was forecast to what actually happened and write plain language explanations of the gap. Capital spending and zero-based budgeting use these forecasts to test whether a proposed purchase or expense still makes sense.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Rolling forecasts and variance explanation are the most mature, because they rely on structured financial data that a model can read directly. External signals in revenue models are useful but fragile, since a correlation that held last quarter can break without warning. Capital spending decisions are not solved by AI, the tools can rank scenarios but cannot judge strategic fit or risk appetite. Zero-based budgeting is partly automated for expense classification, yet the decision to keep or cut a program still sits with a human manager. Honest limits include data gaps, model drift, and the fact that rare events like a supply shock or a lawsuit are hard to predict from history.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with Rolling Forecasts, because that page explains the basic engine that the other pages depend on. External Signals in Revenue Models shows how outside data gets added to that engine, and what can go wrong when the signal is noisy. Variance Analysis and Explanation is the feedback loop, it tells you why the forecast missed and which assumptions to fix. Capital Spending Decisions takes the forecast and applies it to long term purchases, where the cost of being wrong is highest. Zero-Based Budgeting is the expense side counterpart, it uses the same forecast to force every line item to justify itself from zero each period.
